text: You have num courses courses and a list of prerequisite pairs a, b, meaning a is a direct prerequisite of b. For each query u, v, tell me whether u is a prerequisite of v — directly or indirectly. The graph is a DAG.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm reading the direction right — a pair a, b is an edge from a to b, so a comes first. And u being a prerequisite of v means there's a path from u to v. Is that right?
How many queries, and how big is the graph? That tells me whether to answer each query on the fly or precompute everything up front.
Courses up to about a hundred, but queries can be up to ten thousand.

Then precomputing all-pairs reachability once beats re-searching per query. Let me run through an example. Say four courses, with edges zero to one, one to two, and one to three. Then zero reaches everyone, one reaches two and three, but two and three reach nothing — they're siblings, with no path between them.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. This problem reminds me of computing the transitive closure of a DAG, and there are two clean ways. Floyd-Warshall — a triple loop that sets reach i j if reach i k and reach k j. That's cubic, trivial to write, and fine at a hundred courses. Or a topological sweep that propagates prerequisite sets forward, in O of V times V plus E, which scales better on sparse graphs. I'll go with the topological one — it reuses Kahn's in-degree ordering, so every course is processed only after all of its prerequisites.

Here's the plan. One: build the graph from a to b and count in-degrees. Two: run Kahn's queue from every course with in-degree zero. Three: when I pop u, for each edge u to v, mark u as a prerequisite of v, copy every prerequisite of u over to v, and push v once its in-degree hits zero. One thing worth flagging — the propagation is only correct because I process in topological order. When I pop u, every prerequisite of u has already been processed, so the whole column, table i u, is final. That's exactly what lets me copy it forward to v without missing anything. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
The topological one is good. Code it up.

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I build the edges from a to b with in-degrees, seed the queue with the zero in-degree courses, and pop them in order. For each edge u to v, I set table u v to true, decrement v's in-degree, and then loop over every course i: if i is a prerequisite of u, it becomes a prerequisite of v too. At the end each query is a single table lookup. One thing worth flagging — that inner loop over i is where the O of V factor comes from: for each edge I copy up to V prerequisites forward. That's the whole cost of building all-pairs reachability.

Let's dry-run the code on my example: edges zero to one, one to two, one to three, so the queue starts with zero. The row that matters is popping one: for edge one to two I set table one two, and since zero is already a prerequisite of one, zero inherits two as well; the same happens for three. Now the queries. Zero, three is true, through one. Two, three is false — siblings, no path. Zero, two is true. Answer: true, false, true. The sibling case is the interesting one: propagation only flows down the arrows; it never links two nodes that merely share a parent.

Let me think about complexity here. Time to build the table is O of V times V plus E — each edge triggers an O of V propagation. Each query is constant time, so the total is O of V times V plus E, plus Q. Space is O of V squared for the table. Oh, one more thing — at a hundred courses I could just as well write Floyd-Warshall in three lines; it's cubic but needs no graph build and no topological order. And if V were huge, I'd store each course's prerequisite set as a bitset and propagate with a single OR.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You spotted this as transitive closure and chose to precompute because queries dominate. You explained precisely why topological order is what makes the forward propagation correct. And you caught the sibling case — that reachability isn't the same as sharing a parent. Good work.
